subject: religious-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which statement reflects a religious argument used against euthanasia?
options: Only God should decide the time of death, as life is sacred
questions.explain: Some believers argue that, since life is God-given, only God should decide when it ends.

options: God being made known through direct experiences such as visions, dreams or scripture
Knowledge of God only from nature
questions.explain: Special revelation is God revealing himself directly, for example through scripture, visions or prophets.

questions.q: How might a believer respond to the argument that science explains the universe without God?
options: By arguing science explains how things happen, while God explains why they exist
questions.explain: Many argue science and religion answer different questions, so science does not automatically rule out God.

questions.q: What is a 'near-death experience' often claimed to be by some believers?
options: Evidence of an afterlife or spiritual realm
questions.explain: Some interpret near-death experiences as glimpses of an afterlife, though others give natural explanations.

questions.q: A believer says a miracle convinced them God is real. Which argument does this illustrate?
questions.explain: The argument from miracles uses apparently supernatural events as evidence for God.

questions.q: Which view best reflects a 'pro-life' position on abortion?
options: That abortion is always the woman's free choice
That the unborn child has a right to life from conception
That the foetus is not alive at any stage
That life only begins at adulthood
questions.explain: The pro-life position holds that human life begins at conception and should be protected.

questions.q: Which view supports the use of animals in some circumstances within many religious traditions?
options: That animals must never be touched
That animals have no role in creation
That humans have stewardship over animals and may use them responsibly
questions.explain: Many traditions allow responsible use of animals while still teaching kindness and care towards them.

questions.q: Which is a possible religious response to the problem of evil?
options: Suffering may result from human free will or serve a greater purpose
questions.explain: Free-will and 'soul-making' theodicies argue suffering can be reconciled with belief in God.

questions.q: What does the term 'sanctity of life' mean?
options: That life is sacred and God-given, and should be respected
That life has no special value
That life is purely a matter of chance
questions.explain: Sanctity of life is the belief that life is holy, God-given and deserving of special respect.

questions.q: What is the 'problem of evil' as an argument against God?
options: That suffering exists, which seems hard to reconcile with an all-loving, all-powerful God
That the universe is too ordered
questions.explain: The problem of evil questions how an all-good, all-powerful God could allow suffering.

options: The painless ending of a life to relieve suffering
questions.explain: Euthanasia refers to deliberately ending a life, usually to relieve incurable suffering.

questions.q: What does the Christian idea of 'dominion' over creation traditionally mean?
options: Humans are given responsibility and authority to care for creation
Humans must never use natural resources
questions.explain: Dominion is often interpreted as responsible authority and care, not the right to exploit.
